newsitem.title: ITALY: Albania force set to deploy from April 14.
newsitem.headline: Albania force set to deploy from April 14.

text.p: Italy said on Friday that a multinational security force of up to 6,000 troops it plans to lead into Albania should begin deploying in the week starting April 14.

The Foreign ministry named the date after senior diplomats from eight countries certain to take part or considering sending troops met in Rome to establish a political steering committee for the operation.
"The committee took note that the force should be deployed in Albania in the week beginning April 14 in parallel with the arrival of international humanitarian aid," a statement said.

The force, authorised but not organised by the United Nations, will secure key ports and transport routes to protect the delivery of European humanitarian aid from armed gunmen and lawless mafias in the anarchic Balkan state.

It has Security Council approval to operate for an initial three months, up to early elections planned for the end of June, but Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta was quoted on Friday as saying the mission may need to stay on longer.

"The U.N. has set this time scale but it is clear that if this military and electoral cycle requires four or five months, it is probable that the U.N. will extend the mandate," Andreatta told La Stampa newspaper.
Italy is expected to provide between 2,000 and 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Spain 300 and Romania 400. Austria and Denmark say they are also considering participation.

All eight countries are represented on the diplomats' committee, which will report regularly on the mission to the Security Council and keep the European Union and Europe's OSCE security forum informed.
Albania, Europe's poorest country, has been rocked by unrest since January when shady investment schemes into which much of the population had pumped their life savings began to collapse.
Much of the south has been run by rebel "salvation committees" since central control collapsed in mid-March after the protests mushroomed into insurrection.
Thousands of Albanians have seized small arms from state weapons depots plundered as police and soldiers took flight.

The mission will be the first of its kind to be led by Italy, which is eager to restore stability after 13,000 Albanians fled across the Adriatic to its shores last month in a flotilla of ramshackle boats.
Its organisation of the task force was complicated last week by the sinking of a refugee boat after a collision with an Italian corvette engaged on dissuasive patrol in the Adriatic.
Albania says at least 80 people died, many from the rebel-held southern port of Vlore. It and Durres port as well as Tirana airport will be key bridgeheads for the aid mission.

The Foreign Ministry confirmed that the force would be led by an Italian general, 57-year-old Luciano Forlani. He commands Italy's Third Armoured Corps and is a former commander of an Italian division attached to NATO rapid intervention forces.
Italy's chief of defence staff, Admiral Guido Venturoni, said the operation would require 5,000 to 6,000 men on the ground "to restore a minimum of order in a reasonable time".
"Let's be clear about this. The situation there is already improving a great deal. But if there weren't risks there would be no reason to go there," Venturoni said.
"If anyone attacks us it is clear that we will respond," he told Corriere della Sera newspaper.
